Senses.PreferredTarget: stir a thought and at once deviate
AlternateTargets: move a thought and immediately go astray
raise a thought and at once miss
Senses.Explanation: Literally, “stir a thought and at once deviate.” The phrase's Zen-specific deployment is a compact verdict and answer, frequently paired with “form an intention and at once err” (擬心即差), but the corpus explicitly refuses to turn its negative wording into mere mental stillness. Huangbo says, “it is just this; stir a thought and at once deviate” (當體便是，動念即乖), then compares what he has described to measureless space. Linji pairs “form an intention and at once err” with the headword and immediately continues with the person who understands not being apart from what is before the eyes (不離目前). Shimen Cizhao quotes the pair and adds: “not intending and not moving, one is doing business in dead water” (不擬不動，正在死水裏作活計). Huanglong Huinan gives the parallel correction: “not intending and not moving is no different from wood and earth; a traveling monk must obtain a turning phrase” (不擬不動，土木無殊，行脚人須得轉身一句). In direct questions, Tianyin answers “What is the body of things?” (如何是法身) with the phrase, while Linye Qi answers “How, finally, should one head toward it?” (畢竟如何趨向) with it and answers the follow-up “what about when thought does not move?” with “the eyebrows are above the eyes” (眉毛在眼上). The record thus bends an ordinary warning about a wayward thought into a portable Chan verdict while its own corrections exclude “do not think” as a complete gloss.
Senses.Note: The common parallel begins with either “form an intention” (擬心) or “raise the mind” (舉心), followed by “at once err” (即差). The entry does not infer why moving thought deviates; it records the phrase's question-answer and verdict deployments and the texts' explicit dead-water, wood-and-earth, and eyebrow replies.

Senses.Explanation: A person recognized as an heir or successor in a teaching lineage. The term occurs 10,572 times in 168 allowlisted texts and is the principal genealogical heading in lamp records: “sixteen lineage heirs of Master Shoushan Nian,” or a counted collateral heir of Daoxin. Narratives recognize or predict a person as an heir, direct questions ask whose heir someone is, and memorial accounts restrict who may be called an heir. The role can be absent and is not limited to ordained monks: one heading names a lay successor of a lay teacher. Chan records use this person-label to construct the teacher-successor roster; a heading establishes lineage structure but does not attribute every exchange beneath it to the teacher.
Senses.Note: Primary person-role sense. Split from lineage succession or affiliation as a relation/status. The separate verb means “inherit the lineage” (嗣法).

Occurrences.Kwic: 汝州首山念禪師法嗣一十六人
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Lineage heading in the Continued Transmission of the Lamp: "sixteen lineage heirs of Master Shoushan Nian of Ruzhou." This is a catalogue label, not a speaker turn.

Occurrences.Kwic: 祖知是法嗣。以時尚未至。

Senses.Explanation: The succession relation or lineage affiliation itself, rather than the person who is an heir. Catalogues append people “whose lineage succession is not detailed” (未詳法嗣者); public questions ask from whom a master obtained lineage succession (師今得法嗣何人); and a messenger carries a written succession document (法嗣書). A single “lineage heir” gloss cannot describe an unknown affiliation or a succession document without changing the referent.
Senses.Note: The recurrent question “from whom did you obtain lineage succession?” (得法嗣何人) must not be paraphrased globally as “obtain lineage heirs.” The related verbal construction is “inherit the lineage from X” (嗣法於X) in its own entry.

Occurrences.Kwic: 未詳法嗣者，附此。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Catalogue note in the Abridged Continuation of the Compendium of Five Lamps: "those whose lineage succession is not detailed are appended here."

Occurrences.Kwic: 問：祖祖相傳傳祖印，師今得法嗣何人？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public question asks from whom the master received lineage succession, not whom he acquired as an heir.

Occurrences.Kwic: 專使文詳持法嗣書到師於法座前受書
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A messenger brings a written succession document, received before the teaching seat.

AlternateTargets: the eye that selects the teaching
Senses.Explanation: The eye of or for the teaching. One direct definition says, 'nowhere not pervasive and nowhere not clear; therefore it is called the eye of the teaching.' In a recorded case, a monk asks what the eye of the teaching is and receives, 'the eye of the teaching has no flaw.' The productive phrase 'an eye that selects the teaching' appears in challenges to distinguish black from white and in the requirement that a lineage teacher possess such an eye. Transmission narratives also contain the pure eye of the teaching within an entrustment formula. These definitions, questions, compounds, and transmission uses establish a teaching faculty or criterion, not the person Fayan Wenyi.
Senses.Note: The headword has 5,130 occurrences in 380 allowlisted texts. The larger correct-eye-of-the-teaching compounds account for many hits and have their own entries or cross-references. The title-name Fayan is handled separately below.

Occurrences.Kwic: 無處不遍、無處不明，故謂之法眼。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Qianyan's record directly defines why it is called the eye of the teaching.

Occurrences.Kwic: 曰如何是法眼曰法眼無瑕
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A raised Jiashan case asks what the eye of the teaching is and answers that it has no flaw.

Occurrences.Kwic: 具擇法眼者，試為我緇素看。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: An address asks one equipped with an eye that selects the teaching to distinguish black and white.

Occurrences.Kwic: 吾以清淨法眼．涅槃妙心．實相無相．微妙正法。將付於汝。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A transmission narrative includes the pure eye of the teaching in an entrustment formula.

Occurrences.Kwic: 夫為宗師，須具擇法眼始得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A direct statement says that a lineage teacher must possess an eye that selects the teaching.

Senses.Explanation: The title-name Fayan identifies Fayan Wenyi. Catalogue headings count the lineage heirs of Great Fayan Wenyi of Qingliang in Jinling, commentaries introduce his turns with 'Fayan Yi said,' and a biography heading names Chan Master Fayan Wenyi of Qingliang before narrating his travels with Shaoxiu and Fajin. These personal predicates and roster relations identify a lineage person, not the eye or faculty described in the common noun sense.
Senses.Note: Fayan lineage occurs 134 times, the full name Fayan Wenyi 24 times, and the quotation formula Fayan said 179 times. This is a proper-name collision rather than a master-specific innovation in the common noun.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: A catalogue heading counts thirteen lineage heirs of Great Fayan Wenyi.

Occurrences.Kwic: 法眼益云：雲門氣勢甚大

Occurrences.AttributionNote: An independent biography heading names Chan Master Fayan Wenyi of Qingliang before narrating his journey with two companions.

Senses.Explanation: Literally the body's or person-shaped term (身) formed with "teaching, standard, or law" (法): here, "teaching-body," attested 6,058 times in 376 allowlisted texts. This English target follows the Chan record's own comparisons rather than importing a glossary definition. Qianyan places three word explanations together: a robe displays the teaching and so is a "teaching-robe" (法衣); "a person can enlarge the Way, therefore it is called teaching-body" (人能宏道，故謂之法身); and being everywhere and clear is called the "teaching-eye" (法眼). Other records give deliberately different predicates. Weilin calls it "each person's originally present own nature" (當人本有之自性). Huanglong says, "the teaching-body has no form; responding to things, it manifests form" (法身無相，應物現形), then raises his whisk and calls that the teaching-body before laughing. A Five Lamps exchange answers the question with "a flower in the sky, a heat shimmer" (空華陽焰). The Ancestral Hall Collection answers it by repeating that "all activities are the teaching-body's function" (一切施為，盡是法身用).
Senses.Note: The corpus does not reduce the word to one theoretical proposition. It asks about the teaching-body, its "function" (法身用), its "side" (法身邊), and "the matter beyond the teaching-body" (法身向上事). The Old Venerables Record even says the teaching-body has "two kinds of illness" (法身兩般病): reaching it while attachment to the standard remains, with one's own view still present and sitting at its side, is the first. Frequent forms include "pure teaching-body" (清淨法身, 487 occurrences), "the teaching-body has no form" (法身無相, 141), "the teaching-body speaks" (法身說法, 27), "the teaching-body's side" (法身邊事, 202), "master of the teaching-body" (法身主, 132), and "the teaching-body's function" (法身用, 23).

Occurrences.Kwic: 遂豎起拂子云。拂子豎起。謂之法身。豈不是應物現形。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Huanglong raises his whisk and says, "the whisk raised upright is called the teaching-body; is this not responding to things and manifesting form?" He then laughs, making the enacted correction part of the witness.

Occurrences.Kwic: 夫法身者，即當人本有之自性也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Weilin's explicit local definition: "the teaching-body is each person's originally present own nature."

Occurrences.Kwic: 人能宏道，故謂之法身；
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Qianyan's word explanation: "a person can enlarge the Way, therefore it is called teaching-body." The record's name has no safe exact roster link.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如何是法身。師曰。空華
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Under the Jiangxi Daoyi heading: "What is the teaching-body?" The teacher says, "a flower in the sky..."; the following words complete the paired image as "a heat shimmer."

Occurrences.AttributionNote: An Ancestral Hall Collection exchange: "All activities are the teaching-body's function. What is the teaching-body?" The teacher repeats, "all activities are the teaching-body's function." The structural heading is insufficient for a safe roster link.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問如何是法身曰法身無相
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A raised Jiashan case: "a monk asked, 'What is the teaching-body?' He said, 'the teaching-body has no form.'" Because this is a later case citation with several speakers, it remains unlinked.

Occurrences.Kwic: 又法身亦有兩般病得到法身為法執不忘己見猶存坐在法身邊是一
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Room instruction in the Old Venerables Record: "the teaching-body also has two kinds of illness. Reaching the teaching-body while attachment to the standard is not forgotten, one's own view still remains, and one sits at the teaching-body's side—this is one." The local speaker is not safely recoverable from the nearest structural head.

Occurrences.Kwic: 舉：「法身說法，青青翠竹盡是法身，未是提綱拈掇時節。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Record of Yunmen, room instructions; Yunmen raises the saying 'the teaching-body speaks; the green bamboo is entirely the teaching-body' and immediately says it is not yet the moment for bringing up and handling the matter. This anchors the productive 'teaching-body speaks' deployment without turning it into a second referent.

Occurrences.Kwic: 夫法身者理絕玄微，不墮是非之境，此是法身極則。如何是法身向上事？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Ancestral Hall Collection; a traveler states a local account of the teaching-body's limit and asks, 'What is the matter above the teaching-body?' This anchors the productive boundary phrase as an object of public questioning, not a second referent of the base term itself.
